content: The University of Chester is located in Chester, United Kingdom. It was originally established in 1839 as Chester Diocesan Training College by prominent members of the Church of England, including future Prime Ministers William Gladstone and Lord Derby. This institution was the first purpose-built teacher training college in the UK, making it one of the oldest higher education institutions in the country. The initial cohort consisted of 40 student teachers. In 1842, William Gladstone inaugurated the college's original buildings, which were situated just outside Chester's city walls on the Parkgate Road site. This location remains the main campus of the University today. In 1910, the college began its affiliation with the University of Liverpool, and by 1930, it became an official affiliated college. This partnership allowed Chester students to receive qualifications awarded by Liverpool and access its facilities, a practice that continues to this day. The institution continued to grow steadily, and by the 1960s, it was considered for university status as part of the UK's expansion of higher education following the Robbins Report. However, these plans did not materialize. Despite this, the college expanded its offerings and admitted women for the first time in 1962. In 1963, it was renamed Chester College of Education. In 1974, the college broadened its academic scope beyond teacher training to include Bachelor of Arts and Bachelor of Science degrees. Reflecting this diversification, it was renamed Chester College of Higher Education. The 1990s saw further development, including the establishment of the School of Nursing and Midwifery (now the Faculty of Health and Social Care) and the introduction of new programs such as Bachelor of Theology degrees, Higher National Diplomas (HNDs), and postgraduate courses, including master's and doctoral degrees. A £10 million campus improvement program was also initiated during this period. By 1995, the institution gained the title University College Chester. However, in 1999, government regulations required university colleges to have their own degree-awarding powers, leading Chester to revert to the name Chester College of Higher Education. In 2002, the college expanded further by acquiring the higher education faculty and campus of Warrington Collegiate Institute. In 2003, Chester was granted degree-awarding powers, allowing it to reclaim the title University College Chester. Finally, in 2005, it achieved full university status and became the University of Chester. In 2007, the university was authorized to award research degrees by the Privy Council. The University of Chester operates across multiple campuses. The main campus, covering 23 acres, is located on Parkgate Road, just north of Chester's historic city walls. It features a mix of Victorian-era buildings, such as the Old College with its chapel, and modern facilities like the Binks Building, which opened in 2003. The campus includes amenities such as a fitness center, swimming pool, bar, and shops. Due to space constraints, some departments have relocated to nearby off-site locations, all within walking distance. For example, the Department of English is housed in a Grade II-listed former Victorian vicarage, while the Department of History occupies the eighteenth-century Blue Coat School and the Cheshire Military Museum at Chester Castle. The university also has a smaller campus in Warrington, located in the Padgate area. This campus originated as a World War II camp for Canadian officers and now includes the North West Media Centre, which collaborates closely with Granada Television. Additionally, the university maintains smaller facilities, such as those at hospitals for nursing students, across Cheshire and The Wirral. The University of Chester is organized into eight faculties, which are further divided into academic departments. These faculties include Applied and Health Sciences, Business, Management and Law, Arts and Media, Education and Children's Services, Health and Social Care, Humanities, Social Sciences, and Life Long Learning. The Faculty of Life Long Learning incorporates the Centre for Work Related Studies, which operates across all faculties. The university also hosts several research centers. The student body consists of approximately 15,000 individuals, most of whom are from the UK. A significant portion of the students are mature learners, and there are twice as many female students as male, partly due to the popularity of nursing, midwifery, and teaching programs. The university also has a small number of international students, supported by an active exchange program. The academic staff includes 569 members, many of whom engage in research and publish their work through the university's own publishing house, Chester Academic Press. The Chester Students' Union (CSU) provides various services and facilities, including union bars, shops, sports clubs, and non-sporting societies. Each campus has its own sports teams, many of which compete in British Universities and Colleges Sport (BUCS) competitions. The union is managed by a combination of full-time staff, part-time student staff, and elected volunteers. The Executive Committee, which includes three sabbatical officers, oversees the union's operations and serves as its trustees. The CSU is affiliated with the National Union of Students. The University of Chester is well-regarded for its teacher training, nursing, and sports science programs. Its strong connections with local businesses and involvement in community events, such as the Chester Literature Festival, enhance its reputation within the region. The university's profile has also been indirectly boosted by the popularity of the television show Hollyoaks, which is set in a fictional college in Chester. The university's coat of arms, granted in 1954, features a shield with St. George's cross, a golden wheatsheaf representing Cheshire, and an open book symbolizing learning. The crest includes a bishop's mitre and crossed swords, reflecting its Church of England origins and ties to Cheshire. The Latin motto, qui docet in doctrina, translates to he that teacheth, on teaching, though the university prefers the interpretation let the teacher teach. The coat of arms has undergone various adaptations and is part of the university's current logo. Notable alumni include environmental campaigner Klaus Armstrong-Braun, television presenter Jim Bowen, international athletes such as John Carleton and Jo Fletcher, and children's author Roderick Hunt. The university has also been associated with prominent faculty members, including theologians Prof. Ron Geaves and Rev. Canon Anthony Thiselton, as well as novelist Alan Wall.
